lines.en: What every skilled negotiator knows is that listening is more powerful than speaking.
It is better to understand the other side's needs before you present your own demands.
Not until both sides feel they have gained something is a deal truly successful.
However tempting it may be to win every point, a good negotiator knows when to compromise.
Were you to accept our first offer, we would be prepared to sign the contract today.
The agreement is said to have taken six months of quiet negotiation to reach.
What persuaded the investors was not the presentation, but the honesty with which the risks were explained.
Little did the buyer suspect that the seller was ready to accept a much lower price.
It is rarely the loudest voice in the room that wins the negotiation.
Should both parties refuse to move, the discussion will go nowhere.
What both sides finally agreed on was a solution neither had imagined at the start.
It is a mistake to reveal your bottom line before you understand the other side's priorities.
Only when the deadline approached did the two companies find the flexibility they had claimed was impossible.
Were we to increase the order by twenty percent, could you improve the price accordingly?
However strong your position may seem, a negotiation that humiliates the other side rarely lasts.
